artiest/the-sugarhill-gang.text:
The Sugarhill Gang brought rap to a large audience for the first time. The trio was put together in 1979 in Englewood, New Jersey, by Sylvia Robinson. With her husband Joe Robinson she had founded the label Sugar Hill Records. The rappers were Michael 'Wonder Mike' Wright, Guy 'Master Gee' O'Brien and Henry 'Big Bank Hank' Jackson. They did not come from the scene in The Bronx where hip hop had originated.

Rapper's Delight was released in September 1979. The long 12-inch version lasts almost a quarter of an hour. Nothing was sampled: a studio band replayed the groove of Good Times by Chic. Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards of Chic threatened legal action and, in a settlement, received a credit as composers. The lyrics, too, were not entirely original. Big Bank Hank borrowed many of his verses from the notebook of Grandmaster Caz. In America the song reached number 36 on the Billboard Hot 100, the first rap single in the top 40 there.

European hits such as Apache and 8th Wonder followed, but in 1985 the trio broke up. Big Bank Hank died in 2014. Rapper's Delight showed that rap could sell on record, and that gave Sugar Hill Records the room for more serious work. In 1982 the label released The Message by Grandmaster Flash & The Furious Five. The recipe, an existing groove with rap over it, later became the basis of hip hop with the sampler. In 2011 Rapper's Delight was inducted into the National Recording Registry of the Library of Congress.
artiest/the-sugarhill-gang.listen: In Rapper's Delight, listen to the bass line: that is not the Chic record, but a studio band replaying Good Times. Notice how the three rappers take turns working through long verses, while that groove runs on for almost a quarter of an hour.

artiest/the-supremes.text:
The Supremes were Motown's most successful group. They began in 1959 in Detroit as The Primettes: four girls from the Brewster-Douglass housing projects, among them Diana Ross, Mary Wilson and Florence Ballard. In 1961 the group signed with Motown, on condition that they chose a different name. Ballard picked The Supremes from a list that Berry Gordy gave her.

The first singles sold poorly. The breakthrough came with the songwriting team Holland-Dozier-Holland. Where Did Our Love Go was released in June 1964 and in August spent two weeks at number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Four more number ones in a row followed. The sound was clear and danceable, with an emphatic beat and Ross as a restrained lead singer. In all, The Supremes had twelve number 1s on the Hot 100. In 1967 Ballard was replaced by Cindy Birdsong, and the group was from then on called Diana Ross & the Supremes. Someday We'll Be Together (1969) was the last number 1.

In 1970 Ross left for a solo career, and Jean Terrell took her place. When Mary Wilson also went solo, the group stopped in 1977. The Supremes were the clearest proof that Motown's approach worked: Black music, carefully packaged, that was also bought by a white teenage audience. Their story lives on in the Broadway musical Dreamgirls (1981), which is loosely based on the group. In 1988 Ross, Wilson and Ballard were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-supremes.listen: Where Did Our Love Go begins with stomping on every beat, listed on the recording as 'foot stomping', together with handclaps. Then listen to how Diana Ross sings low and calm and the other two Supremes answer with 'baby, baby'.

artiest/the-surfaris.text:
The Surfaris are an American surf band from Glendora, California, formed in 1962. The original line-up consisted of Ron Wilson on drums and vocals, Jim Fuller on lead guitar, Bob Berryhill on rhythm guitar and Pat Connolly on bass. In the autumn of 1962 the schoolboys Fuller and Connolly rehearsed with Berryhill, and they met Wilson the same evening at a school party. That was how the band was born. The saxophonist Jim Pash joined later.

In the winter the four wrote and recorded Wipe Out, an instrumental. It came out in January 1963 on a small label, was picked up by Dot in April 1963 and reached the Hot 100 in June. On the B-side was Surfer Joe, which followed in August. It became an international hit and sold more than a million copies. The group went on to release albums such as The Surfaris Play and Wipe Out in 1963, and Fun City, U.S.A. in 1964.

Wipe Out is best known for its opening: before the music starts, Berryhill's father breaks a board next to the microphone, like a breaking surfboard, followed by a crazy laugh and the words Wipe Out. Then comes Wilson's energetic drum solo, one of the best known in pop history. In 2019 the Surfaris were given a place in the Musicians Hall of Fame and Museum.
artiest/the-surfaris.listen: Listen to Wipe Out and notice the opening, with the broken board and the laugh. Then try to follow the drum solo and to hear how the guitars keep playing around it.

artiest/the-tallis-scholars.text:
The Tallis Scholars are a British professional chamber choir, founded in 1973 by Peter Phillips and named after the composer Thomas Tallis. Phillips was an organ scholar at Oxford at the time and asked members of the chapel choirs of Oxford and Cambridge to sing Renaissance music together. The first concert was on 3 November 1973 in Oxford. After ten years the ensemble became professional. Usually there are two singers to a part, with a core of about ten singers, and they sing sacred music a cappella from the period of roughly 1450 to 1600.

Since 1980 they have recorded for their own label Gimell Records, which Phillips founded together with Steve Smith. Well-known recordings are Allegri's Miserere in 1980, Josquin's Missa Pange lingua and Missa La sol fa re mi, which became Gramophone Record of the Year in 1987, and Taverner's Missa Gloria tibi Trinitas. They brought the work of Tallis, Palestrina, Byrd and Victoria to a wide audience and also sang Russian church music and contemporary composers such as Arvo Pärt and Eric Whitacre. In 1994 they sang Allegri's Miserere in the newly restored Sistine Chapel, and in 2000 the choir performed in New York with Paul McCartney.

The sound is clear and transparent, because every voice can still be followed within the rich polyphony. The ensemble set an example for younger groups, such as The Sixteen and the Gabrieli Consort. In 2013 it was elected to the Gramophone Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-tallis-scholars.listen: Listen to Allegri's Miserere and notice the high solo voice that rises above the choir. Can you hear how the voices weave through each other as separate lines and yet together form a single sound?

artiest/the-tallis-scholars-en-peter-phi.text:
The Tallis Scholars are a British professional vocal ensemble for early music, founded in 1973 by Peter Phillips. Phillips studied music and was at that time an organ scholar at St John's College, Oxford. He asked members of the chapel choirs of Oxford and Cambridge to form an amateur ensemble for Renaissance music. The first performance was on 3 November 1973 in the church of St Mary Magdalen in Oxford. After ten years of concerts the group became professional. Usually there are two singers to a part, with a core of ten singers, singing a cappella, without instruments.

The group performs some seventy times a year in Europe, North America, Asia and Australia. In 1994 it sang Allegri's Miserere in the newly restored Sistine Chapel. In 1999 it toured China and in 2000 it performed in New York with Paul McCartney. Since 1980 it has recorded for its own label Gimell Records, which has released more than sixty CDs. After a Gramophone Award in 1987 the Tallis Scholars are regarded as one of the best ensembles for Renaissance polyphony. In 2013 they received a place in the Gramophone Hall of Fame.

Polyphony means that several independent melodic lines sound at the same time. The singing of the Tallis Scholars is clear and pure, so that you can follow every voice. In School of Rock they sing Ave Maria... virgo serena by Josquin and the Kyrie from the Missa Papae Marcelli by Palestrina.
artiest/the-tallis-scholars-en-peter-phi.listen: Listen to the Kyrie from Palestrina's Missa Papae Marcelli. Notice how the voices enter one by one and together form a calm, continuous sound in which you can hear the text clearly.

artiest/the-temptations.text:
The Temptations are an American vocal group from Detroit, formed in 1961 from two local groups: Otis Williams, Melvin Franklin and Elbridge Bryant of the Distants and Eddie Kendricks and Paul Williams of the Primes. They began as the Elgins and signed in 1961 with Berry Gordy of Motown, who gave them the name Temptations. In the first years they had little success, so that they were called the Hitless Temptations. That changed when Smokey Robinson began writing for them and David Ruffin replaced Bryant in 1964. With Ruffin on lead, My Girl, written by Robinson, became their first number one in the United States in 1965.

In 1966 Norman Whitfield took over production, after the success of Ain't Too Proud to Beg. He steered the group away from Robinson's ballads towards a harder, horn-heavy soul in the vein of James Brown. Hits from that period were Beauty Is Only Skin Deep and I Wish It Would Rain. After Ruffin left in 1968, Dennis Edwards came in. With him Whitfield worked on the psychedelic soul of Cloud Nine, I Can't Get Next to You and Ball of Confusion. Cloud Nine earned the first Grammy for a Motown act in 1969. Just My Imagination and Papa Was a Rollin' Stone followed later.

The group stood out for its five-part harmony, meticulous choreography and smart clothes. Between line-ups the lead singers often changed, and the music moved with the times, from doo-wop and ballad to funk and socially conscious soul. In 1989 the Temptations were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. Otis Williams is the last original singer and keeps the group alive.
artiest/the-temptations.listen: Listen to My Girl and notice the bass line that opens it, and the way the five voices alternate. Can you hear how Ruffin's lead sounds warm and rough at the same time?

artiest/the-three-degrees.text:
The Three Degrees is an American female group from Philadelphia, formed around 1963 when the first members were still in high school. Although there have been many singers over the years, the group has always remained a trio. The original members were Fayette Pinkney, Shirley Porter and Linda Turner. In 1963 Janet Harmon and Helen Scott replaced Porter and Turner. The producer and songwriter Richard Barrett discovered them and had them record their first song, Gee Baby (I'm Sorry). In 1966 Sheila Ferguson joined, and in 1967 Valerie Holiday.

That line-up of Pinkney, Holiday and Ferguson became the most successful. In 1974 they sang on TSOP (The Sound of Philadelphia) by MFSB, which topped the American Hot 100. That same year the group had a big international hit with When Will I See You Again. In Britain the group had thirteen hits in the top fifty between 1974 and 1985. Pinkney left in 1976. In 1979 Woman in Love reached number three in the United Kingdom. Ferguson began a solo career in 1986.

The Three Degrees stand for the soft, silky side of Philadelphia soul, with three voices that complement each other. Their work brought that American style to a European audience, above all to the British charts.
artiest/the-three-degrees.listen: Listen to TSOP (The Sound of Philadelphia) and notice the places where the three female voices come in. Can you hear how they complement the orchestra?

artiest/the-time.text:
The Time was an American funk band from Minneapolis, formed in 1981 under a clause in Prince's contract with Warner Bros. that allowed him to recruit and produce other artists. Prince wanted a pop-funk group that would continue the style of his own early albums while he himself went in other directions. He built the band around an existing Minneapolis funk collective, Flyte Tyme, with Jimmy Jam, Terry Lewis and Jellybean Johnson, among others. Morris Day, a childhood friend of Prince, took the place of the singer Alexander O'Neal and found a comic foil in Jerome Benton.

The band released four albums in the 1980s, including The Time in 1981, What Time Is It? in 1982 and Ice Cream Castle in 1984. The tone was light and humorous, with a strong influence from Funkadelic, Parliament, James Brown and Sly Stone. Hits were Get It Up, Cool, 777-9311, Jungle Love and The Bird. On the debut album Prince played almost everything himself, under the name Jamie Starr, and Day had to follow Prince's guide vocal precisely. A rivalry grew with Prince's own band, The Revolution. The group appeared in the film Purple Rain. Jam and Lewis were fired in 1983 and became one of the most successful producer duos of the 1980s and 1990s.

In 1985 the group broke up, and in 1990 it got together for Graffiti Bridge and the album Pandemonium, with the hit Jerk Out. Later the band played as Morris Day and the Time, and under the name Original 7ven Condensate appeared in 2011. The Time belongs to the core of the Minneapolis sound.
artiest/the-time.listen: Listen to Jungle Love and notice the bouncing synthesizer and Morris Day's playful singing. Can you hear how the band mixes funk and new wave with a wink?

artiest/the-tokens.text:
The Tokens were an American doo-wop group from Brooklyn, New York. They began in 1955 at Abraham Lincoln High School under the name Linc-Tones. The first line-up included Neil Sedaka and Hank Medress, and Jay Siegel joined in 1956. Sedaka and Howard Greenfield wrote much of the early material, so that the group was different from the many teenage groups that only did covers. Sedaka left the group in 1958 for a solo career. In 1960 the group got its best-known name and line-up, after the thirteen-year-old Mitch Margo and his brother Phil had joined.

In 1961 the group reached number fifteen on the Billboard Hot 100 with Tonight I Fell in Love. Then came The Lion Sleeps Tonight on RCA Victor, an adaptation of Mbube by the South African singer Solomon Linda from 1939. The song spent three weeks at number one in the United States, reached number eleven in Britain and, like the first single, went gold. Between 1962 and 1970 nine more songs followed on the Hot 100, such as I Hear Trumpets Blow and Portrait of My Love, always with Siegel on lead. From 1963 they also worked as producers for groups such as The Chiffons and The Happenings, with their own company Bright Tunes.

The Tokens remained successful in the time of the British Invasion. In 1972 a new recording of The Lion Sleeps Tonight with Robert John reached number three. The rights to the song were later litigated, as was the name of the group. Siegel and the Margo brothers still perform with their own versions.
artiest/the-tokens.listen: Listen to The Lion Sleeps Tonight and notice the repeating little chorus beneath the lead, the high singing on top and the calm accompaniment. Can you hear how a South African melody is transformed by a doo-wop group?

artiest/the-tony-williams-lifetime.text:
The Tony Williams Lifetime was a jazz fusion group led by the drummer Tony Williams. The band began in 1969 as a power trio with John McLaughlin on electric guitar and Larry Young on organ. The name possibly refers to Williams's first album as a bandleader, Life Time from 1965. The debut Emergency! was a double album from 1969 that many jazz fans rejected at the time because of its heavy rock influences and that is now regarded as a fusion classic. On the second album, Turn It Over from 1970, Jack Bruce played bass and sang.

After that the line-up changed constantly. On Ego in 1971 Ted Dunbar played guitar and Ron Carter bass, and the last record for Polydor, The Old Bum's Rush in 1973, had an entirely new line-up, with vocals, electronic keyboards and a lighter soul-jazz approach. In 1975 Williams put together a new Lifetime with Allan Holdsworth on guitar, Alan Pasqua on piano and Tony Newton on bass. For Columbia they made Believe It in 1975 and Million Dollar Legs in 1976. Other line-ups without major releases followed later.

The hard, electric sound of the first Lifetime, with organ, sharp guitar and Williams's driving drums, made a great impression on the nascent fusion scene. Musicians of The Allman Brothers Band listened to it a lot, and Andy Partridge of XTC names Emergency! as his favourite album. After Williams's death in 1997 tributes followed, such as Spectrum Road with Jack Bruce in 2012.
artiest/the-tony-williams-lifetime.listen: Listen to a track from Emergency! and notice Tony Williams's drums: can you hear how they lie beneath the organ and the guitar like a constantly shifting engine?

artiest/the-united-states-marine-band.text:
The United States Marine Band is the premier ensemble of the United States Marine Corps. Congress established the band on 11 July 1798, making it the oldest American military band and the oldest professional musical organisation in the country. Since 1801 it has carried the nickname The President's Own. This arose when President John Adams invited the band to play at the presidential palace on New Year's Day, and Thomas Jefferson asked for it for his inauguration. Since then the band has played at every American presidential inauguration.

The band plays some five hundred times a year, at state funerals, state visits, White House dinners, parades and concerts. On summer Friday evenings it performs at the parades at the Marine Barracks in Washington. The group has about 130 members, who apply through a rigorous audition and serve four years as service members, but do not have to go through basic training. Besides the main band there is a chamber orchestra and there are smaller ensembles. Every autumn the band goes on a tour of the country, a tradition that began in 1891.

The most famous leader was the composer John Philip Sousa. During his time as director he wrote marches such as Semper Fidelis, and led the band in the late nineteenth century. In this way the Marine Band has contributed to the repertoire of the American march and to popular wind music.
artiest/the-united-states-marine-band.listen: Listen to a Sousa march played by this band, such as Semper Fidelis, and notice the clear brass sound and the tight, driving beat. Can you hear how the melody is passed around among the trombones and trumpets?

artiest/the-upsetters.text:
The Upsetters were the house band of the Jamaican reggae producer Lee Scratch Perry. The name comes from Perry's nickname Upsetter, after his song I Am the Upsetter, a musical settling of scores with his former boss Coxsone Dodd. The band was active from 1968 to 1986, with a changing line-up.

The Upsetters were originally Gladdy's All-Stars, led by the pianist Gladstone Anderson, and made the international hits Live Injection and Return of Django. The double A-side Return of Django with Dollar in the Teeth reached number five in the British chart in November 1969. When the All-Stars had no time for a tour of England, the band the Hippy Boys took their place. That line-up is the studio band most associated with the name. It consisted of the guitarist Alva Lewis, the organist Glen Adams and the brothers Aston Family Man Barrett on bass and Carlton Barrett on drums. Under Perry's leadership they backed Bob Marley, above all on the albums Soul Rebels and Soul Revolution Part II. After 1972 Perry brought in other musicians, such as Boris Gardiner and Sly Dunbar, for the Black Ark.

The Upsetters show how in Jamaica a producer could form a band of his own. They laid the foundation for the later Wailers, and their records for Perry are regarded as building blocks of reggae and dub. Dread Lion belongs to the later period at the Black Ark.
artiest/the-upsetters.listen: Listen to Dread Lion and notice the bass and the drums. Can you hear how the rhythm section carries the song?

artiest/the-velvet-underground.text:
The Velvet Underground was formed in 1964 in New York around the singer and guitarist Lou Reed and John Cale. Cale came from the avant-garde and had worked with the composer La Monte Young. The guitarist Sterling Morrison and the drummer Moe Tucker completed the line-up. In November 1965 the group took its name. The artist Andy Warhol became their manager and added the German singer Nico. The band sold few records, but left a long afterlife.

The debut The Velvet Underground & Nico was released in March 1967, with a banana by Warhol on the sleeve. The album got no further than number 171 on the American album chart. Reed wrote openly about heroin, prostitution and sadomasochism. Many radio stations refused to play the album. Venus in Furs is based on a novel by Leopold von Sacher-Masoch. Cale brought the drone: long, sustained notes on an electric viola. White Light/White Heat (1968) was harder and rougher still. After that Cale was fired. On The Velvet Underground (1969) and Loaded (1970) the band sounded calmer. Reed left in August 1970.

Brian Eno said in 1982 that the first album sold only 30,000 copies in its early years, but that everyone who bought one started a band. Punk, post-punk and alternative rock went back to their raw sound. The group also resonated behind the Iron Curtain: in Prague they were the great example for The Plastic People of the Universe. In 1996 the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-velvet-underground.listen: In Venus in Furs John Cale plays electric viola: not a melody, but a grating drone that hangs beneath the vocal throughout the song. Notice also Lou Reed's out-of-tune guitar and Moe Tucker's slow, heavy rhythm.

artiest/the-vines.text:
The Vines are an Australian rock band from Sydney, formed in 1994. Craig Nicholls met the bassist Patrick Matthews at a McDonald's in a suburb of the city. Together with the drummer David Olliffe they first played under the name Rishikesh, after the Indian town where the Beatles visited an ashram in 1968. When newspapers kept misspelling that name, Nicholls chose The Vines, as a tribute to his father, who was in a local band. Nicholls became the main songwriter and was the only constant in all the line-ups.

The debut album Highly Evolved came out in 2002, recorded with the producer Rob Schnapf in Los Angeles. The album reached number eleven in the United States and went platinum in Australia. Get Free earned the group an ARIA Award for Breakthrough Artist and was ranked highly by NME. That year they appeared on the cover of Rolling Stone and NME, and they were grouped with a wave of bands with The in their name, such as The Strokes, The Hives and The White Stripes. Winning Days in 2004, Vision Valley in 2006, Melodia in 2008, Future Primitive in 2011, Wicked Nature in 2014 and In Miracle Land in 2016 followed.

The sound is described as a mixture of 1960s garage rock and 1990s alternative rock. Vision Valley consists of short, direct songs and barely lasts thirty minutes. The band was part of the return of guitar rock in the early 2000s.
artiest/the-vines.listen: Listen to Get Free and notice the contrast between the quiet verses and the screaming chorus. Can you hear the influence of garage rock and grunge?

artiest/the-vipers-skiffle-group.text:
The Vipers Skiffle Group, later simply The Vipers, was one of the most important British skiffle groups of the mid and late 1950s. The group began in the spring of 1956 in central London as a trio of singers and guitarists: Wally Whyton, Johnny Martyn and Jean Van den Bosch, who was replaced in 1958 by Freddy Lloyd. Later that year a rhythm section was added, with Tony Tolhurst on bass and John Pilgrim on washboard. They played regularly at the Soho club 2i's Coffee Bar, where they sometimes jammed with Tommy Steele.

In September 1956 they auditioned for George Martin of Parlophone and were given a record contract. Their second single, Don't You Rock Me Daddy-O, reached the British top ten in early 1957. The song is a variant of the folk song Sail Away Ladies, which Uncle Dave Macon had recorded in the 1920s. Their version of Maggie May also appeared that year, which the BBC banned because of its sexual lyrics. Lonnie Donegan on the Pye label was their competitor. He copied Whyton's arrangements and reached higher chart positions with the same song and with Cumberland Gap. Their version of Cumberland Gap also reached the top ten, and Streamline Train followed.

The Vipers are important because they helped shape British skiffle and prepared the way for beat. Martin later said that working with them taught him how to work with informal, enthusiastic musicians. Members of The Shadows also came from their circle.
artiest/the-vipers-skiffle-group.listen: Listen to Don't You Rock Me Daddy-O and notice the washboard and the acoustic guitars. Can you hear how few instruments it takes to make so much rhythm?

artiest/the-wailers.text:
The Wailers, later Bob Marley and the Wailers, was a Jamaican group for ska, rocksteady and reggae. It was formed in 1963 when the self-taught Peter Tosh met the singers Bunny Wailer and Bob Marley. First they were called the Teenagers, then the Wailing Rudeboys and the Wailing Wailers, before they arrived at the Wailers. In 1964 Simmer Down was at the top of the Jamaican chart. The song was recorded at Studio One, with the rhythm section of the Skatalites, and called on Jamaica's rude boys to calm their anger. It contributed to Jamaican music no longer imitating foreign artists, but capturing the life and spirit of Jamaica.

The first album, The Wailing Wailers, appeared in 1965. In 1970 and 1971 they worked with the producers Leslie Kong and Lee Scratch Perry, with Perry's studio band the Upsetters. In 1972 they signed with Island Records. In 1973 Catch a Fire and Burnin' followed. Tosh and Wailer left in 1974 because of dissatisfaction with the label and ideological differences. Marley continued with a new line-up, including the I-Threes, and died of cancer in 1981, after which the group stopped. Well-known songs are Trenchtown Rock, Stir It Up, Get Up, Stand Up and I Shot the Sheriff.

The Wailers brought reggae to the world. Their music rests on a heavy, melodic bass and on short guitar accents on the offbeat, with voices singing about injustice, freedom and everyday life. In this way reggae went from being a Jamaican style to an international sound, and Marley became one of the most famous pop figures in the world.
artiest/the-wailers.listen: Listen to Stir It Up by Bob Marley and the Wailers. Notice the difference between the bass, which is melodic and heavy, and the guitar, which plays short and on the offbeat.

artiest/the-weavers.text:
The Weavers were an American folk quartet from Greenwich Village in New York. Lee Hays, Pete Seeger, Ronnie Gilbert and Fred Hellerman founded the group in November 1948, after Hays and Seeger had earlier founded the Almanac Singers. The name comes from the play Die Weber by Gerhart Hauptmann, about the uprising of the Silesian weavers in 1844. The group sang traditional songs from all over the world, but also blues, gospel, children's songs, workers' songs and American ballads.

After a successful performance at the Village Vanguard they signed with Decca. In 1950 came their big hit, Goodnight, Irene by Lead Belly, with Tzena, Tzena, Tzena on the flip side. The record spent thirteen weeks at the top of the chart and was the first folk arrangement to have so much success. On Top of Old Smoky, So Long, It's Been Good to Know Yuh, Kisses Sweeter than Wine and Rock Island Line were also made known by them. They encouraged the audience to sing along, and Seeger sometimes called out the words ahead of each line. On the early recordings they still had strings and an orchestra behind them.

In the time of the communist witch-hunt the members were blacklisted. Seeger and Hays had to appear before a committee of the House of Representatives, the records disappeared from Decca's catalogue and in 1952 the group stopped. In December 1955 it got together for a sold-out concert at Carnegie Hall, after which Vanguard followed. Seeger left in 1958, and the group stopped in 1964. Their success opened the way for the folk revival of the 1960s. In 2006 they received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.
artiest/the-weavers.listen: Listen to Goodnight, Irene and notice the calm, almost rocking melody and how four voices carry the chorus together. Can you hear the orchestral accompaniment that lies beneath the voices in the early recordings?

artiest/the-weeknd.text:
The Weeknd is the stage name of Abel Tesfaye, born in 1990 in Toronto to Ethiopian immigrants. He grew up in the Scarborough neighbourhood. Tesfaye shows how a pop star can arise in the age of streaming: first anonymously online, then the stadiums. In 2021 he performed at the Super Bowl halftime show, the first Canadian solo artist to be given that performance.

At the end of 2010, without a name or a face, he put three songs on YouTube. In 2011 three mixtapes followed: House of Balloons, Thursday and Echoes of Silence. House of Balloons in particular sounded dark: alternative R&B about drugs, parties and the loneliness of the night. In 2012 the three mixtapes appeared together as Trilogy. Beauty Behind the Madness (2015) contained the hits Can't Feel My Face and The Hills, and on Starboy (2016) he worked with the French duo Daft Punk. The album After Hours (2020) brought Blinding Lights, written by five writers including Max Martin and Oscar Holter, who also produced it with him.

Blinding Lights sounds as if it was recorded in the 1980s, with synthesizers that critics compared with a-ha and OMD. In 2021 Billboard declared it the best-performing hit in the history of the Hot 100. It spent 57 weeks in the top ten. On Spotify it became the most-streamed song and the first to reach four billion. In this way The Weeknd connects Max Martin's hit factory with the sound of synth-pop and new wave.
artiest/the-weeknd.listen: Blinding Lights (2019) opens straight away with a synthesizer riff that is already a hook, followed by a tight drum machine rhythm in the style of the 1980s. Notice how little else happens: the riff and the beat carry the whole song.

artiest/the-west-coast-get-down.text:
The West Coast Get Down is an American jazz collective from Los Angeles. The members all grew up in Los Angeles County and first came together in 1993 in the Multi-School Jazz Band of the music teacher Reggie Andrews in Watts. The group includes the saxophonist Kamasi Washington, the bassists Miles Mosley and Stephen Thundercat Bruner, the drummers Ronald Bruner Jr. and Tony Austin, the pianist Cameron Graves, the keyboard player Brandon Coleman, the trombonist Ryan Porter and the multi-instrumentalist Terrace Martin. As schoolchildren they played in Washington's garage, nicknamed the Shack, and later in clubs such as the World Stage in Leimert Park.

In 2008 Mosley began a residency at the Piano Bar in Hollywood, which lasted eight years, and in 2009 the collective was officially founded there. In December 2011 the members recorded for thirty days in a row at Kingsize Soundlabs in Echo Park, the KSL Sessions, from which some 190 tracks came. Many of them later appeared on solo albums, including Washington's The Epic in 2015. That year Martin, Washington, Mosley and Ronald Bruner contributed to Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly, the album that made them known to a large audience.

The collective is called the Wu-Tang Clan of jazz. It is praised for freshening up jazz for younger listeners, with a broad, cinematic sound and a connection to hip hop and soul. The members now mainly go their own ways, often with one another, and a joint album under this name is, according to Washington, an idea for the future.
artiest/the-west-coast-get-down.listen: Listen to Kamasi Washington's saxophone sound in a track from The Epic and notice how choir and strings enlarge the spacious, cinematic sound. Can you hear the connection with hip hop and soul?

artiest/the-white-stripes.text:
The White Stripes were an American rock duo from Detroit, Michigan, formed in 1997. Jack White played guitar and keyboards and sang, Meg White sat behind the drums and also sang. They were among the leaders of the indie and garage rock revival of the 2000s. In the late 1990s they first tried to break through in Detroit. After that they made six studio albums.

The first big success came with the third album, White Blood Cells in 2001. Elephant followed in 2003 and brought the first Grammys, with Seven Nation Army, which became a sports anthem and the group's signature song. Get Behind Me Satan from 2005 was an experiment, Icky Thump from 2007 returned to the blues. In 2011 the group stopped. They won six Grammys and a Brit Award.

The music is deliberately raw and simple, with influences from garage rock and blues. Recordings were made to sound lo-fi on purpose. The group kept up a mysterious image, with a colour scheme of red, white and black on all the sleeves, and a fondness for the number three. Their success shows that two people and minimal material could have an enormous impact in the digital age.
artiest/the-white-stripes.listen: Listen to Seven Nation Army and notice the riff at the start. Can you hear how such a bare line carries the whole song, and how the drums only come in later?

artiest/the-who.text:
The Who was formed in 1964 in London out of an earlier group, The Detours. The classic line-up consisted of the singer Roger Daltrey, the guitarist Pete Townshend, the bassist John Entwistle and the drummer Keith Moon. With The Kinks and the Small Faces, The Who was the band of the mods, the young people with scooters, sharp suits and a taste for soul.

After I Can't Explain came My Generation in 1965, which reached number 2 in England and became the mods' anthem. On stage Townshend smashed his guitar and Moon kicked over his drum kit. Townshend began to think bigger and bigger. Tommy (1969) was a rock opera about a deaf, dumb and blind boy, and that same year the band played at Woodstock. Live at Leeds (1970) is regarded as one of the best live albums in rock. On Who's Next (1971) synthesizers are central, which was still new in rock at the time. Quadrophenia (1973) is a concept album about a young mod in the 1960s.

Moon died in 1978 and Entwistle in 2002; Daltrey and Townshend carried on. The film Quadrophenia (1979), with the riots between mods and rockers in Brighton, made mod culture popular again. Townshend also inspired The Beatles: when McCartney read that Townshend called I Can See for Miles (1967) the loudest and rawest song by The Who, he wanted to top it and wrote Helter Skelter. The Britpop bands of the 1990s looked back to The Who and the mods. In 1990 the band was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-who.listen: In My Generation the key goes up three times, from G through A and B flat to C, and with each step the tension rises. Listen also to John Entwistle's short bass guitar solos, still unusual at the time, and to the guitar feedback with which the song collapses instead of fading out.

artiest/the-wild-bunch.text:
The Wild Bunch was an English sound system and a loose collective of musicians and DJs from the Bristol neighbourhoods of St Paul's, Montpelier and Bishopston. The name comes from Sam Peckinpah's 1969 western. The group began in 1982 as a sound system on the Bristol scene, with Grantley Marshall, known as Daddy G, and Miles Johnson, DJ Milo, as the main DJs. In 1984 they asked the young graffiti artist Robert Del Naja, 3D, to join. He became one of the MCs. Later Claude Williams and, in 1987, Adrian Thaws, known as Tricky, among others, joined.

As pioneers of sound system culture they played all night in clubs and in abandoned warehouses. In 1986 they played at the St Paul's Carnival and signed with 4th and B'way, a label of Island Records. That year they toured Japan, after which DJ Milo stayed on to work there. They held sound clashes with other sound systems, including Soul II Soul. In 1985 the single Tearin Down the Avenue was recorded and in 1988 Friends and Countrymen appeared. By then Del Naja, Marshall and Andrew Vowles had already formed Massive Attack, and in 1989 The Wild Bunch no longer existed. Nellee Hooper went to London and became a producer and remixer, for Madonna, U2 and Björk, among others.

The Wild Bunch mixed hip hop, punk, R&B and reggae in a single performance. Their preference for slower rhythms and ambient, electronic atmospheres laid the foundation for the Bristol sound, which later became trip hop. The collective showed how a sound system with loose DJs and MCs could eventually give rise to an entire scene.
artiest/the-wild-bunch.listen: Listen to Unfinished Sympathy by Massive Attack, a group that emerged from The Wild Bunch. Notice the slow tempo and the spacious, dark atmosphere that belongs to the Bristol sound.

artiest/the-winstons.text:
The Winstons were an American funk and soul group from Washington, D.C. The band consisted of Richard Lewis Spencer on tenor saxophone and lead, Ray Maritano on alto saxophone, Quincy Mattison on guitar, Phil Tolotta on organ, Sonny Pekerol on bass guitar and the drummer Gregory C. Coleman. They were a mixed group, and that was precisely why it was hard to get gigs in the South. In 1970 the group stopped. They also played as the backing band of The Impressions.

In 1969 their best-known record appeared. On the A-side was Color Him Father, a soul song that reached number seven on the Billboard Hot 100, sold more than a million copies and went gold. It won a Grammy for best R&B song in 1970. On the B-side was Amen, Brother, an instrumental. Halfway through, Coleman plays a drum solo of a few bars, which later became known as the Amen break. Love of the Common People also reached the Hot 100 in 1969.

That short drum solo became the most sampled recording in the history of electronic music. Musicians used it in thousands of songs in genres such as breakcore, drum and bass, hip hop, jungle, big beat and industrial. In this way the B-side of a small soul group has had a great influence on the dance music of later decades.
artiest/the-winstons.listen: Listen to Amen, Brother and wait for the drum solo halfway through. Notice Gregory Coleman's rhythm: can you hear why this little passage has been used as a sample so often?

artiest/the-wolverines.text:
The Wolverines were an Australian country rock band from Tamworth in New South Wales. Darcy Leyear on guitar and vocals, John Clinton on drums and vocals and Chris Doyle on keyboards and vocals founded the group in 1994. They remained active until 2021 and were known to some as the Bad Boys of Country. The name comes from an encyclopedia, which described the wolverine as a nearly extinct, nocturnal animal regarded by some people as a pest.

The group's albums are Feel the Need to Ride in 1999, Wolverines and Roses in 2002, Making Tracks in 2004 and Good Ol' Boys in 2010. Some songs have coarse and sexual lyrics, others are sincere tributes. One of their hits is 65 Roses, written by Lee J. Collier, about a boy who could not pronounce the words cystic fibrosis, his sister's illness. The Wolverines turned the original country waltz in three into a country rock song in four. The single was meant to raise awareness of the disease and money for Cystic Fibrosis Australia.

The group played at festivals all over Australia, for 40,000 people at the Gympie Muster, and for American marines in Okinawa. In 2003 and 2007 it sailed along the coast and gave a concert at every stop for underprivileged children, under the name Wolverines Sail for Kids. The first voyage raised more than 35,000 dollars for research into the disease.
artiest/the-wolverines.listen: Listen to 65 Roses and notice how the song sounds like robust country rock in four-four time. Can you hear that the lyrics about a sick child stand in contrast to the robust sound?

artiest/the-wrecking-crew.text:
The Wrecking Crew was a loose collective of American session musicians from Los Angeles, who in the 1960s and 1970s played on countless studio recordings, including hundreds of hits. At the time they were rarely credited on the sleeve. They had no official name then. The drummer Hal Blaine said that older musicians came up with that nickname because they feared that rock 'n' roll would wreck the music industry, although the bassist Carol Kaye disputes that story. The musicians usually had a background in jazz or classical music and were excellent sight-readers.

In 1962 they formed the house band for producer Phil Spector's Wall of Sound at Gold Star Studios. After that they were the most sought-after session musicians in the city. They played for Jan and Dean, Sonny and Cher, The Mamas and the Papas, the Carpenters and Frank and Nancy Sinatra, among others. Sometimes they also played under the name of rock groups, for example on Mr. Tambourine Man by The Byrds in 1965, on the first two albums by The Monkees and on Pet Sounds by the Beach Boys in 1966. The members included the drummers Hal Blaine and Earl Palmer, the saxophonist Steve Douglas, the guitarist Tommy Tedesco and the keyboard player Larry Knechtel, later of Bread. Leon Russell and Glen Campbell became solo stars themselves.

In Los Angeles studio time was expensive, so songs had to be recorded in as few takes as possible. The Wrecking Crew could do that in any style. Their work remained largely unnoticed until Blaine's memoirs in 1990. In 2000 Blaine and Palmer were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, in 2007 the whole group followed into the Musicians Hall of Fame, and in 2008 a documentary about them appeared.
artiest/the-wrecking-crew.listen: Listen to Be My Baby by The Ronettes, a Phil Spector record. Notice the thick, reverberating sound of many instruments at once, which is characteristic of the Wall of Sound in which the Wrecking Crew played.

artiest/the-yardbirds.text:
The Yardbirds are an English blues rock band that formed in London in 1963 around the singer and harmonica player Keith Relf. With Paul Samwell-Smith, Chris Dreja, Jim McCarty and the guitarist Top Topham they began in the suburbs of south-west London. The name possibly comes from On the Road by Jack Kerouac, or is a nickname of the saxophonist Charlie Parker. They succeeded the Rolling Stones as house band of the Crawdaddy Club in Richmond and played Chicago blues by Howlin' Wolf, Muddy Waters and Bo Diddley. Topham was replaced by Eric Clapton, and manager Giorgio Gomelsky guided the group.

With For Your Love, written by Graham Gouldman, the first big hit came in 1965. Clapton thought it too commercial and left for John Mayall. Jeff Beck succeeded him, on the recommendation of Jimmy Page. With Beck came Heart Full of Soul, Shapes of Things and Over Under Sideways Down, the last on the album Yardbirds, known as Roger the Engineer. Beck experimented with fuzz, feedback and Middle Eastern influences, and the group sometimes sang like Gregorian monks. The rave-up, in which the tempo doubled, became their trademark. Page then joined in, and Happenings Ten Years Time Ago and Little Games followed.

The Yardbirds are regarded as pioneers of psychedelic rock and early hard rock. The early careers of Clapton, Beck and Page gave the group a great reputation. After the break-up in 1968 Page founded Led Zeppelin, and Relf and McCarty started Renaissance. In 1992 the Yardbirds were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/the-yardbirds.listen: Listen to Shapes of Things and notice Jeff Beck's guitar solo, which rises above the band with feedback and an Eastern-sounding line. Can you hear how a pop single begins to sound psychedelic here?

artiest/thelonious-monk.text: Thelonious Monk grew up in the San Juan Hill neighbourhood of Manhattan and as a boy played in churches and at rent parties. There he heard the stride piano of James P. Johnson, who lived nearby, and he admired Duke Ellington, whose music he played on an entire album in 1955. In the early 1940s he was pianist in the house band of Minton's Playhouse. Monk played with angular rhythms, dissonant chords and silences. He wrote pieces that became standards, such as 'Round Midnight, Straight, No Chaser and Epistrophy. For a long time he was seen as an eccentric. Only after his 1957 performances with John Coltrane at the Five Spot did he gain wide recognition; in 1964 he was on the cover of Time.
artiest/thelonious-monk.listen: Notice the 'wrong' notes and the pauses: they are meant exactly as they are.

artiest/them.text:
Them was a Northern Irish rock band from Belfast, formed in April 1964. Van Morrison was looking for musicians for a new R&B club at the Maritime Hotel, and made a new group out of the Gamblers, a band from East Belfast of Ronnie Milling, Billy Harrison and Alan Henderson. The schoolboy Eric Wrixon played piano. Morrison played saxophone and harmonica and sang. The name comes from the 1950s horror film Them! At the club the group played without a fixed programme, and Morrison improvised: it was there that his song Gloria took shape, and sometimes it lasted twenty minutes.

Decca signed the group. The first recordings in London were made in July 1964, with session musicians alongside the band. Baby, Please Don't Go reached number ten in Britain in 1965, and on the B-side was Gloria, which became a standard of garage rock. Here Comes the Night, written and produced by Bert Berns, reached number two. Mystic Eyes reached the top forty in the United States. The first album was The Angry Young Them in 1965, followed by Them Again in 1966. In Los Angeles they played together with The Doors in 1966, and they jammed a long version of Gloria.

After a dispute over money the group broke up in 1966 and Morrison began a solo career. Henderson carried on with other line-ups, until 1972. The combination of blues and garage rock had a great influence on later bands, such as The Doors. In 1999 the recording of Gloria was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.
artiest/them.listen: Listen to Gloria and notice the simple, repeating guitar riff and how Morrison spells out the letters of the name. Can you hear how few chords it takes to create so much tension?

artiest/theo-uden-masman.text:
Dirk Theodoor Uden Masman was born in 1901 in Cheribon in the Dutch East Indies and died in 1965 in The Hague. He was trained at the Nederlandsche Academie voor Muziek of Siegfried Blaauw in The Hague. In 1926 he founded the big band The Ramblers, a jazz and dance orchestra that continued until 1964. Masman remained the bandleader. His radio performances always ended with Farewell Blues and his announcement that the orchestra would be back.

In the 1930s and 1940s The Ramblers were a popular radio big band and helped make jazz known in the Netherlands and Belgium. During the war the orchestra played for the broadcaster controlled by the Germans and at pro-German gatherings, which led after the liberation to a ban on performing. Masman was not allowed to lead the orchestra for a year. According to the Dutch source, the band received lighter punishments because members also helped Jewish former bandleaders who were in hiding. A song from 1941, Dag Schatteboutje, is heard in the 2016 film Riphagen.

Masman had a good feel for what the public wanted and in this way brought the orchestra to great popularity after the war, also with a programme of its own at the VARA. At the end of the 1950s interest declined, and the last broadcast was on 11 April 1964. He wrote dozens of songs, under his own name and above all as Dick Hansen, such as Zeeman, o zeeman from 1950 and 'k Heb maling aan geld from 1953.
artiest/theo-uden-masman.listen: Listen to Dag Schatteboutje by The Ramblers and notice the smooth, swinging sound of the big band. Can you hear how the horns share the melody with the singer?

artiest/theo-uden-masman-en-the-ramblers.text: The pianist Theo Uden Masman founded The Ramblers in 1926, which grew into the best-known Dutch dance orchestra of the 1930s. The band played in hotels, on radio and in films, and made many records. The orchestra played a mixture of dance music and jazz in the style of the American bands of the time. In 1935 and 1937 the American tenor saxophonist Coleman Hawkins, who was then working in Europe, made records with The Ramblers in the Netherlands. That was a high point for Dutch jazz before the war. During the occupation the orchestra had to abide by the rules of the German occupier, who distrusted jazz. After the war the band continued to play on the radio until 1964.
artiest/theo-uden-masman-en-the-ramblers.listen: Hear how a Dutch dance orchestra plays the American swing of the 1930s.

artiest/theon-cross.text: The tuba player Theon Cross from London learned to play through Tomorrow's Warriors and played in Sons of Kemet with Shabaka Hutchings. He does not use the tuba as an accompanying instrument from the brass band, but as bass in dance music: heavy, rhythmic lines that recall grime and dub. He also played with Moses Boyd and Nubya Garcia. On his album Fyah (2019) the tuba is central, with Nubya Garcia on saxophone. In this way he showed that the tuba has a place of its own in the new jazz.
artiest/theon-cross.listen: Listen to the tuba as the bass line of a dance track.

artiest/thibaut-de-champagne.text:
Thibaut de Champagne was born in 1201 in Troyes and was Count of Champagne from his birth. His father died less than a week before, and his mother Blanche of Navarre ruled as regent until he came of age in 1222. In 1234 he became King of Navarre as Theobald I, succeeding his uncle. In 1239 he led the Barons' Crusade to the Holy Land, which was militarily not very glorious but, through negotiations with the Ayyubids, led to the recovery of Jerusalem. He died in 1253 in Pamplona.

Outside politics he was a well-known trouvère, a poet and singer from the north of France. Many of his songs have survived, some of them with music. In the French court life of the thirteenth century, such poetry about courtly love belonged to chivalric culture, and a nobleman who wrote songs himself was no exception. Thibaut also wrote a poem for his wife while he was staying in Acre.

His importance for music history lies in the songs that have been handed down. Because a lord like him had his own texts and melodies written down, we have one of the richest collections of medieval trouvère repertoire. That makes him a bridge between politics, chivalric culture and early Western song, long before popular music as we know it.
artiest/thibaut-de-champagne.listen: Listen to a song by Thibaut de Champagne and notice the single melodic line without accompaniment or with a simple instrumental backing. Can you hear how the singing follows the lines of the poem?

artiest/thijs-van-leer.text:
Thijs van Leer, born in 1948 in Amsterdam, is a Dutch musician and the founder of the rock band Focus, in which he sang and played organ and flute. He grew up in a musical family. His father was a classically trained flautist, his mother a singer. Van Leer was already playing piano at the age of three and was given a flute at eleven. He discovered jazz, above all through records by Miles Davis, and thought that jazz and classical music could be combined in rock. He studied art history, took lessons at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam and studied flute and composition in Geneva. Rogier van Otterloo taught him orchestration and arranging.

From 1967 to 1969 he sang and played in the cabaret of Ramses Shaffy. Then he formed Trio Thijs van Leer, which at the end of 1969 continued with the guitarist Jan Akkerman as Focus. The group broke through internationally with Moving Waves in 1971 and the single Hocus Pocus, with its yodelling and whistling. After several albums with changing line-ups he disbanded Focus in 1978, and in 2002 he started the group again. As a solo artist, too, he was successful in the Netherlands, with Introspection in 1972, among others, and he collaborated with other artists. In 2008 he was made a knight in the Order of Orange-Nassau for his services to music.

Van Leer's mixture of classical music, jazz and rock gave Dutch pop music an international face. His flute, his organ and his idiosyncratic voice made Focus unmistakable in the early 1970s.
artiest/thijs-van-leer.listen: Listen to Hocus Pocus by Focus. Notice the flute, the yodelling and the whistling of Thijs van Leer, and the hard guitar playing of Jan Akkerman around them.

artiest/thom-yorke.text: Thom Yorke was born in 1968 in Wellingborough. In 1985 at Abingdon School he started, with schoolmates, the band that later became Radiohead. He wrote his first film score for Suspiria (2018), Luca Guadagnino's new version of the 1977 horror film. Yorke deliberately chose not to refer to Goblin's music for the original film. He drew inspiration from the soundtrack of Blade Runner, from the musique concrète of Pierre Henry and from krautrock from the Berlin of 1977, where the film is set. The London Contemporary Orchestra and Choir play and sing along. The piano song Suspirium was nominated for a Grammy. Later he wrote the music for the Italian film Confidenza (2024).
artiest/thom-yorke.listen: In Suspirium, listen to the waltzing piano accompaniment and Yorke's high, soft voice, and elsewhere to choir and electronics slowly swelling ominously.

artiest/thomas-a-dorsey.text:
Thomas Andrew Dorsey was born in 1899 in Villa Rica, Georgia, the son of a preacher and farmer, and died in 1993. He grew up amid spirituals, hymns and the country blues of an uncle, and in Atlanta learned to play blues on piano in barrelhouses and at parties. In 1919 he moved to Chicago, where he became an arranger and composer and was one of the first musicians to have blues copyrighted. He became pianist and leader of Ma Rainey's band and, as Georgia Tom with the guitarist Tampa Red, recorded the successful It's Tight Like That, which sold more than seven million copies.

After a period of deep depression he devoted himself from 1928 to religious music. Apart from the lyrics he saw no real difference between blues and church music. In Chicago he was for fifty years musical director of the Pilgrim Baptist Church, where he introduced improvisation, clapping, stomping and shouting, even though many churches considered that inappropriate. In 1932 he co-founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses and, with Sallie Martin, started the first publishing house for Black gospel. After the death of his wife and son he wrote Take My Hand, Precious Lord. Peace in the Valley is also his. He is estimated to have written three thousand songs.

Many early gospel singers worked or studied with him, such as Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin, Roberta Martin and James Cleveland. He is called the Father of Gospel Music, although he mainly started a movement that spread gospel blues through the Black churches. According to one author, he combined the good news of gospel with the bad news of the blues.
artiest/thomas-a-dorsey.listen: Listen to Take My Hand, Precious Lord and notice the slow, almost moaning vocal and the blues in the melody. Can you hear how sorrow is turned into a church song here?

artiest/thomas-acda.text:
Thomas Acda, born in 1967 in Amsterdam, is a Dutch cabaret performer, actor, writer and singer. He is best known as one half of the duo Acda en De Munnik. He grew up in the village of De Rijp in North Holland and after secondary school first went to drama school, but soon switched to the Kleinkunstacademie in Amsterdam. There he met Paul de Munnik. In 1993 they graduated with a joint production, for which they received the Pisuisse Prize. After that they split up for a while, and Acda played in the band Herman en Ik, among others.

In 1995 the two got together again for the theatre show Zwerf'On. It was such a success that they put the songs on CD. Since then they moved between music and theatre. The duo came from the theatre and made songs with Dutch lyrics that stood between cabaret and pop music. The song Als het vuur gedoofd is was used in the film All Stars, and every episode of the accompanying television series began with Groen als gras. At the start of 2014 Acda and De Munnik announced that they were stopping as a theatre duo.

Acda also worked as an actor. From 1997 he appeared in films such as All Stars, The Missing Link and Lek, and in the series All Stars he played the goalkeeper Willem. He also appeared in In Oranje, Alles is liefde and Flikken Maastricht. For Alles is liefde he received a Rembrandt award in 2008. For years he was on the panel of the television programme Dit was het nieuws. His work shows how in the Netherlands cabaret, television and pop lie close together.
artiest/thomas-acda.listen: Listen to Groen als gras by Acda en De Munnik. Notice the simple accompaniment and how the lyrics sound narrative and almost spoken, as you would expect in the theatre.
